evidence of a shipping compatibility-mode implementation in Firefox or Safari.
findings.problem: Source 018 (already cited as [11]) states outright that Safari is not anticipated to ship compatibility mode and that Mozilla has not committed, so the draft claims silence where its own cited source speaks.
findings.fix: — and the same intent's availability expectation answers the question directly: Mozilla "is interested in this feature (and has approved all of the spec changes) but has not committed to implementing it yet", while for Apple "it is not anticipated that this feature will ship in Safari since all Apple devices on the market can support the full Core WebGPU spec"; on the same thread Chrome's WebGPU lead added "we don't expect all browsers to ship it ever", describing Firefox as considering it against competing WebGPU priorities [11].

findings.quote:
- **Will Firefox or Safari implement compatibility mode?** Both registered positive standards
  positions [11], but the corpus has no implementation signal — WebKit/Mozilla
  standards-positions entries or tracking bugs would settle it.
findings.problem: This open question is answered by [11] for Safari (not anticipated to ship) and partly for Firefox (considering, not committed), and 'both registered positive standards positions' misstates the source, which says there is no entry for compatibility mode in the standards-positions repos.
findings.fix: - **Will Firefox implement compatibility mode?** Safari is effectively settled: the Blink intent says it is "not anticipated that this feature will ship in Safari" because all shipping Apple devices support core WebGPU, and compatibility-mode apps run unchanged on core-only browsers [11]. Firefox is the open half — Mozilla approved the spec changes but has not committed to implementing, and neither Gecko nor WebKit has an entry for compatibility mode in the standards-positions repos (the "Positive" labels are the intent author's reading of Working Group participation) [11]. A Mozilla tracking bug would settle it.

findings.section: Reading the evidence: where sources disagree
findings.quote:
Two further items are launch-day press coverage of the
Firefox 141 announcement and add no primary facts beyond the Mozilla post [13][14]
findings.problem: Source 019 ([13]) is not pure rehash: it reports the author's own hands-on test on Firefox 141 (a Unity WebGPU game running at barely 30 FPS, dipping to 10-18, with occasional freezes) and the about:config prefs used, which is first-hand evidence of a Firefox limitation the draft omits.
findings.fix:
Two further items are launch-day press coverage of the
Firefox 141 announcement; the linuxiac piece adds no primary facts beyond the Mozilla post [14], while the itsfoss piece adds one hands-on data point — a rotating-cube demo rendered cleanly, but a Unity WebGPU game (Project Prismatic) ran at barely 30 FPS, dipping to 10-18, with occasional freezes, on the Firefox 141 beta with `dom.webgpu.enabled` and `dom.webgpu.allow-present-without-readback` set [13]

findings.section: Chrome and Chromium: broadest reach, platform tail still open
findings.quote:
- **Secure-context only.** `navigator.gpu` is undefined over `http:` or `file:`; the API is
  available only in secure contexts [9].
findings.problem: Listed under limitations 'documented by Chrome itself', which implies a Chrome-specific restriction; MDN [21] documents the secure-context requirement as applying to the whole API in every engine.
findings.fix:
- **Secure-context only.** `navigator.gpu` is undefined over `http:` or `file:`; the API is
  available only in secure contexts [9]. This is a spec-level rule rather than a Chrome
  quirk — MDN states the whole API is available only in a secure context, so Firefox and
  Safari behave the same way [21].

browser, which points at diagnostics as well as correctness [19]. This is a single
